title: Itch.io Deletes 'Terabytes' of AI Slop in to Counter Surge in Game Uploads
content:
Indie game online store Itch.io is facing the same problem that has afflicted a number of major digital storefronts in recent months: AI. Steam’s Next Fest saw more demos than ever, with genAI a significant factor in those numbers. Epic Games can’t help but insist developers be allowed to use AI freely. Alongside them, Itch.io has been facing its own growing issue of AI-generated titles cluttering its service, with the company confirming that the number of games uploaded to the site has as much as doubled in recent months as slop tools become more widespread.
The conversation surrounding Itch.io’s uptick in AI platforms arose after the company posted a graph documenting the number of game pages being created per day on the platform. Between August 3rd and October 30th, this number had roughly doubled from just over 3000 to above 6000 per day. Notably, the company said there was not a similar uptick in downloads and purchases. When one person asked on BlueSky if Itch knew why this was happening, the company replied saying, “Take a guess.”
The company, to its credit, already has a number of policies in place to aid in this situation. In response to a particularly damning image of one user taking over almost an entire page of game uploads with near-identical AI-created games, the company confirmed bulk uploads like this are against current content guidelines and actively de-indexed the lot from search. That being said, Itch states this is not the main cause of the issue: according to Itch, “the increase in the graph is driven by first time uploaders, not bulk uploaders like this.”
Itch staff noted in another social media post that they were “sad” that the platform’s current offers to host content were being abused. In response, the store has already begun to implement new policies, now requiring all uploads in the tabletop (aka physical games), books, comics and soundtracks categories comply with AI disclosures already implemented elsewhere, instructing users to state if these tools have been used, and in what ways. Notably, this is necessary even if the materials were later edited to remove AI-generated elements.
Moderation is also increasing. The company has deleted “a couple terabytes” of AI slop, and is adding a user filter for games with generative AI disclosure filtering—those who don’t wish to see games using these tools won’t have them appear in search.
Is it enough? Some people have responded to Itch.io’s posting throughout the last few days asking why it doesn’t just entirely ban AI content, considering the platform is designed specifically for solo and hobbyist creators. A filtering system won’t please those people. However, the costs of having the kind of moderation necessary to find and remove such content would be quite high if such a policy were implemented, and some in programming fields see AI’s use in coding, even if not in onscreen art, as acceptable.

report.summary: Itch.io says AI-generated game uploads have doubled daily, prompting it to delete terabytes of low-quality content and add AI disclosures and filters.
report.background: Itch.io is an open indie game storefront known for hosting solo and hobbyist creators. In recent months, major digital storefronts have struggled with a surge in generative-AI content: Steam saw record Next Fest demos, and Epic Games has defended developers' freedom to use AI. Itch.io posted a graph showing daily game-page creation roughly doubling from just over 3,000 to above 6,000 between August 3 and October 30, while downloads and purchases did not rise similarly. The platform already had content guidelines against bulk uploads and had de-indexed near-identical AI-generated games, but it says the broader surge is driven mainly by first-time uploaders rather than bulk spammers.
key_points: Itch.io’s daily game-page creation rose from about 3,000 to more than 6,000 between August and October, but downloads and purchases did not show a matching increase. The company’s graph made clear that upload volume and actual player demand are diverging.

Itch.io says the increase is driven mainly by first-time uploaders, not bulk uploaders. It has still de-indexed bulk uploads of near-identical AI-made games, which violate its content guidelines, but that enforcement does not explain the overall surge.

The platform is expanding AI disclosure rules to tabletop games, books, comics and soundtracks. Creators must state whether generative AI was used and how, even if AI-generated material was later edited or removed.
Moderation is increasing: Itch.io has deleted “a couple terabytes” of AI slop and is adding a user filter so people can hide games that disclose generative-AI use from search results.

Some users want a full AI ban, but Itch.io faces high moderation costs and some developers see AI-assisted coding as acceptable. The platform is choosing disclosure and filtering over a blanket prohibition.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Itch.io’s response shows storefronts moving from open experimentation to disclosure, filtering and cleanup. For developers, AI-generated uploads can bury human-made games and make discovery harder, while disclosure rules add administrative work and may stigmatize some projects. For regular users, filters could improve browsing, but detection and enforcement remain uneven. The bigger signal is that platform moderation costs are becoming a central AI policy issue: blanket bans are simple to demand but expensive to enforce, so disclosure systems and user-controlled filters are likely to spread across game stores and other creative marketplaces.
report.tools: Follow Itch.io’s AI disclosure guidelines and its new generative-AI search filter, plus Steam’s AI disclosure policy for comparison. Platform builders can study open-source moderation stacks and Hugging Face content classifiers, though AI detection remains unreliable. Artists may also watch tools like Glaze and Nightshade for protecting visual work.
